newsitem.title: spain: OPINION - Merrill Lynch CM Spain on Amsterdam, EMU.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Merrill Lynch CM Spain on Amsterdam, EMU.

text.p: By Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch Capital Markets Espana

MADRID, June 23 - The Amsterdam Summit which took place on June 16 and 17 has provided some answers but has also left some questions about the future of the European Union, though its overall effect on Spanish markets has been positive.
It was hoped that, during the summit, two key aspects of the future of the EU would be approved.

Firstly, the ratification of the Stability Pact initially agreed at the Dublin summit. Secondly, the Maastricht Treaty reform, which should introduce far-reaching institutional reforms within the Community bodies with a view to preparing the EU for the entry of new members from Eastern Europe.

Regarding the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the most important aspect of the summit was the ratification of the Stability Pact, a demand imposed upon the rest of the member countries by Germany in order to ensure that the budget reduction achievements on the road to the euro are sustained once the third phase of EMU is launched on January 1, 1999.

Although imposing restrictions on the sole instrument of economic policy which the national governments will control is questionable, and despite the fact that the Pact's design offers a high degree of discretion on the issue of sanctions against countries not fulfilling targets, Germany has strong reasons to insist upon such an agreement, bearing in mind that in terms of prices it is historically the most stable of all countries.
Therefore, its currency has great credibility on the financial markets.
German public opinion is reluctant to abandon the mark in favour of a currency of dubious stability if those countries it represents are not sufficiently virtuous in their fiscal policies.

In order to attempt to convince the German electorate that the credibility earned during years of austerity will not be placed at risk with its entry into EMU, the German government has attempted to endow the monetary union with an independent European Central Bank and a sanctioning mechanism (Stability Pact) which strengthens budgetary discipline beyond 1999.

In principle, ratifying the Stability Pact was going to be straightforward at the Amsterdam Summit. However, the unexpected socialist victory in the French elections and the new government's intended social turnaround in its macro-economic policy has changed the French position on the Pact.

Bearing in mind Germany's fierce opposition to a monetary union without a Stability Pact, doubts about the future of the project abounded during the days leading up to the summit, with negative repercussions on the spreads of peripheral countries.
As is usually the case when political considerations outweigh economic criteria, France toned down its stance during the heads of state summit.

Germany has achieved the ratification of the Pact in exchange for a chapter on employment in the new Amsterdam Treaty, which calls on European governments to cooperate in the fight against unemployment and allows financing job creation through European institutions such as EIB and CECA.
In this way, Germany has also avoided the burden of any such policies falling on the Community's budget, thus avoiding also an increase of its contribution towards European coffers.

Additionally, a special summit on employment will be held in the autumn. It is doubtful that these initiatives will result in concrete decisions, which leads one to believe that Germany was the clear winner in the fight for the Pact's ratification. Therefore, the obstacles which arose on the road to EMU were overcome and the project remains on course.
Questions remain fundamentally on the failed institutional reform, which should have set the scene for the entry of new members into the EU.

The agreements here are scarcely ambitious as institutional reforms will remain postponed until the entry of new members. In the remaining chapters, few supra-national initiatives were seen in a summit in which Chancellor Kohl, with his sights set firmly on October's elections, did not give European matters the necessary push for fear of giving the impression that he was neglecting national interests.
The poor results prove, once more, the ambivalence of the process's political momentum.
Political integration remains distant from economic integration on the list of priorities of the European leaders, but political will was what avoided the Amsterdam summit derailing.
However, there are still great differences between the EMU wanted by Germany (austerity, strong euro) and that wanted by France (social policies, inclusion of peripheral countries and weaker euro).

The delicate situation in which the German government finds itself in order to demand greater austerity in foreign countries' accounts, makes it likely that, on this occasion, the French stance will prevail.
The consequences are clear. There will be an EMU in 1999, which will probably include Spain. The Spanish 10-year spread has already taken this into account, falling recently to historical lows.
